ch04.note: The chapter's title, Ikusa ikusa — literally 'war, war' — names the stretch it covers: the Shizugatake campaign and the fall of the house of Shibata, one war treading on the heels of the last. (Printed folio 199.)

A shimenawa is a rope of twisted rice-straw hung with paper streamers, marking off sacred or purified ground; at the New Year one is strung over a doorway to keep the coming year's ill luck out. (Printed folio 200.)
'Bald rat' (hage-nezumi) was Nobunaga's own scornful pet name for Hideyoshi, known from a surviving letter of his; here Goemon borrows it. (Printed folio 201.)

ch04.anchor: Reckonings and loincloths both slip loose from the far end.
ch04.note: A rustic proverb: atekoto to fundoshi wa mukō kara hazureru, 'reckonings and loincloths both come loose from the far side' — what you count on fails of its own accord, and from the direction you least expect. (Printed folio 202.)

A charm muttered to turn away lightning and misfortune. By one tradition the lands (kuwabara, mulberry-field) of a former Sugawara estate were never struck, the thunder-god sparing his own old ground. (Printed folio 202.)

The old lunisolar calendar kept step with the sun by inserting a thirteenth 'leap' month as needed; Tenshō 11 carried a second, intercalary first month, so the year held two New Years. (Printed folio 203.)
A gohei is a ritual wand hung with zigzag paper streamers, used in Shinto to summon or embody a god; Katsuie bore its shape worked in gold as his field standard (umajirushi). (Printed folio 205.)
Hachiman, god of war, was worshipped in syncretic form as a bodhisattva (daibosatsu); his name on a war-banner was held to overawe the enemy. (Printed folio 206.)

ch04.anchor: He had his Iga ration pills by him
ch04.note: The shinobi's hyōrōgan: a compound of dried rice, buckwheat, bonito, dried loach, pickled-plum flesh and steamed pine-bark, rolled into pills said to sustain a man ten days. The recipe that follows is given in momme (about 3.75 grams) and bu (about 3 millimeters). (Printed folio 221.)

The young spearmen decorated for valor at Shizugatake — among them Katō Kiyomasa and Fukushima Masanori — became a fixture of popular history and the stage. As the author notes, nine men were in fact commended; 'seven' was chosen for its ring. (Printed folio 220.)

ch04.anchor: faced a raging tiger with a cross-bladed spear
ch04.note: Katō Kiyomasa's tiger-hunt in the mountains of Korea, with a cross-bladed spear (jūmonji-yari), is among the best-loved episodes of his legend. (Printed folio 220.)

Hideyoshi's celebrated 'Great Return' (ō-gaeshi): on word of the raid he raced some fifty kilometers by night from Ōgaki back to the Shizugatake front, feeding and lighting the road from the villages, and struck before Katsuie's army could turn its success to account. (Printed folio 225.)
Hideyoshi's famous sen-nari byōtan, the 'thousand-gourd' standard: by legend a gourd was added for each victory until the pole bore a golden cluster of them. (Printed folio 227.)

ch04.anchor: in a letter he sent on the eighteenth of December
ch04.note: Luís Fróis (see Chapter 1), the mission's chronicler, described Shizugatake in a genuine dispatch to the Visitor Valignano; Murayama quotes it, then adds — with a wink — that its only possible witness at the castle's heart was Goemon. (Printed folio 237.)

Three stock exemplars of the retainer who dies in his lord's place: Ji Xin, who impersonated Liu Bang so the Han founder could escape Xiang Yu; Satō Tadanobu, who covered Yoshitsune's flight; and Murakami Yoshiteru (Hikoshirō), who died in Prince Morinaga's stead. (Printed folio 239.)

ch04.anchor: famed from her girlhood as the fairest in the realm
ch04.note: Oichi (see Chapter 3), Nobunaga's sister and one of the noted beauties of the age. The portrait the author describes, commissioned by her daughter Yodogimi (the Lady Yodo), survives at the Jimyō-in on Mount Kōya. (Printed folio 246.)
Katsuie's tower at Kita-no-shō was among the first of the great multi-storied keeps, said to rise nine tiers; it burned with him and his household. (Printed folio 243.)
The aristocratic hikimayu: the natural brows were shaved and two lozenge- or moth-shaped brows painted high on the forehead, a court fashion of the age. (Printed folio 248.)

ch04.anchor: a death worse even than crucifixion
ch04.note: Azai Manpukumaru, Oichi's son and the Azai heir, was hunted out after Odani fell in 1573 and put to death by impalement at Kinomoto; the deed is laid variously to Nobunaga's order and, as here, to Hideyoshi's hand. (Printed folio 253.)
The source gives Oichi's age as thirty-seven on folio 246 and thirty-six here; both are rendered as printed. (Printed folio 255.)
